::: {#thm-inverse-bijective}
#### A function has an inverse exactly when it is a bijection

A function $f : A \to B$ (@def-function) has an inverse function (@def-inverse-function)
if and only if $f$ is bijective (@def-bijective).
The graph (@def-graph) of the inverse function is then the inverse relation (@def-inverse-relation) of the graph of $f$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

($\Rightarrow$)
Suppose $g : B \to A$ is an inverse function of $f$.

**Injective.**
If $f(a) = f(a')$, then $a = g(f(a)) = g(f(a')) = a'$.

**Surjective.**
Each $b \in B$ has $b = f(g(b))$, so $b$ is the value of $f$ at $g(b) \in A$.

($\Leftarrow$)
Suppose $f$ is bijective, and let $b \in B$.
Since $f$ is surjective, some $a \in A$ has $f(a) = b$,
and since $f$ is injective, only one $a$ does.
Let $g(b)$ be that $a$.
Then $g : B \to A$ is a function with $f(g(b)) = b$ for every $b \in B$.
For $a \in A$, $g(f(a))$ is the one element $a'$ with $f(a') = f(a)$, which is $a$ itself.
So $g$ is an inverse function of $f$.

**The graph of the inverse.**
In both cases, $f(g(b)) = b$ for every $b \in B$ and $g(f(a)) = a$ for every $a \in A$.
Let $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.
If $g(b) = a$, then $f(a) = f(g(b)) = b$.
If $f(a) = b$, then $g(b) = g(f(a)) = a$.
So $(b, a)$ is in the graph of $g$ exactly when $(a, b)$ is in the graph of $f$.

:::

:::
